title: How to work fly stitch in cross-stitch
subtitle: A small V-shape for leaf veins, feathers, and decorative details
excerpt: Fly stitch is a short V-shaped stitch caught at the base by a tiny straight stitch. In cross-stitch it appears as a decorative detail on leaves, bird feathers, and botanical stems, where a single small V reads more naturally than a row of full crosses.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. William Morris-period embroidery manuals, surface stitch chapter, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A V-shaped stitch formed by coming up at the left arm of the V, inserting the needle to form the right arm, and catching the base of the loop with a small straight stitch.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

content.text: is a short V held in place by a small downward catching stitch at the base of the loop. It appears on cross-stitch charts as a decorative element on leaves, flower petals, and bird feathers, where the V-shape reads more naturally than a full cross would at the same scale.
A single fly stitch needs three entry points on the fabric: the left arm of the V, the right arm, and a small gap below the centre for the catching stitch. On 14-count
the typical fly stitch spans two squares across the top and one square down for the catching stitch. Work in one strand for the most delicate result; two strands give a bolder V.
Come up at the left arm of the V. Lay the
loosely across the surface toward where the right arm will be.
Insert the needle at the right arm position and bring it back up at the centre-bottom, below the midpoint of the two top holes. The needle exits through the loose loop of floss lying on the surface.
Pull the needle through until the V draws up into a neat shape, with the two arms roughly the same length.
Take the needle down just below the base of the V (one to two Aida squares below the exit point) to form the small catching stitch that holds the loop in place.

Pull through to the back with the same light tension as a full cross. The catching stitch should be just long enough to hold the V; a longer catching stitch makes the stitch read as a Y rather than a V.

items.symptom: The V arms are uneven in length
items.cause: The two top holes are not equidistant from the centre-bottom exit point.
items.fix: Count the Aida grid carefully before inserting the needle for the right arm. Both top holes should be the same number of squares from the centre.

items.symptom: The loop slips before the catching stitch is secured
items.cause: Too much tension was applied to the floss before the catching stitch pinned the base.
items.fix: Hold the forming V lightly with a finger while taking the catching stitch down. Release the finger only after the needle is through the fabric.

content.text: Fly stitches work well in groups along a leaf vein or along the edge of a wing. Once comfortable with the individual stitch, try grouping three or four stitches in a fan formation to suggest feathers or a small flower.
